I have farmed this land in Quzhou for over fifty years. My plots total 10 mu on the North China Plain — flat, loamy, alkaline soil, with access to the village's shared tube well. I am 70 and my back is not what it was, so I rely on the village machinery cooperative for sowing and harvest. But my mind is sharp and I have learned what this land needs.

The rotation I have kept my whole life is winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same ground. I will not change this. It suits our climate, our markets, and the soil. Some younger men in the village are experimenting with other crops, but at my age and with my land, reliability matters more than novelty.

**Winter wheat** is already in the ground — I sowed it last October using Kenong 199, an improved variety that handles our dry springs well and has good lodging resistance. I applied base phosphorus and potassium at sowing along with the first nitrogen split. Now in April I am planning the jointing-stage topdressing (urea) and will irrigate twice more — at jointing and grain-filling. I will not irrigate a fourth time. Groundwater here has dropped badly over the decades; I remember when the water table was 5 meters, now it is over 30. Three irrigations is enough for a decent yield if I time them well. I will spray once for powdery mildew and once for aphids near heading. Expect around 480 jin per mu — not the highest in the county, but stable.

**Summer maize** goes in immediately after wheat harvest in June, no-till, directly into the stubble. I use Xianyu 335 hybrid seed. Summer rain handles most of the water need; I only irrigate at emergence if it is dry, and possibly once at silking. Maize requires less of my labor than wheat, which suits me in the summer heat. I apply fertilizer in two splits — base compound at sowing and urea topdress at the 8-leaf stage. One pesticide pass for corn borer is usually enough.

My priority this year: cut one irrigation from wheat compared to last year, see if yield drops. I believe it will not.
